source.title: Classical Statistical (In-Sample) Intuitions Don't Generalize Well: A Note on Bias-Variance Tradeoffs, Overfitting and Moving from Fixed to Random Designs

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including its appendix, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper empirically examines test error across model complexity in linear regression and compares fixed- and random-design prediction, a conceptual test of general double descent using a different setting and measure from deep-network model-wise double descent.
record.gate_note: The paper also discusses earlier findings on effective parameter counts and double descent, but those are attributed to cited work and are not recorded as results of this study. The paper’s own linear-regression sweep and k-NN complexity results are recorded below.
record.test_reason: The paper runs its own linear-regression feature-count sweep and finds double descent only in out-of-sample error. It also argues analytically that a second descent cannot occur in fixed-design in-sample error. Together these restate where the general double-descent curve (V4) can hold. T2 would also be defensible, since the sweep itself reproduces double descent in linear regression.
record.authors_conclusion: Accurate. The authors argue that evaluating models on random-design generalization rather than fixed-design in-sample error is a key, under-discussed reason modern phenomena like double descent appear. Their linear-regression sweep shows double descent out-of-sample only, and they argue it is impossible in-sample.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses a linear-regression feature-count experiment and compares in-sample with out-of-sample prediction; it does not reproduce the original deep-network model-size experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported double-descent shape depends on evaluating out-of-sample rather than in-sample prediction.

fits_no_version.finding: For k-NN estimators on a nonlinear DGP, out-of-sample bias is itself U-shaped in k. Both bias and variance can fall as complexity decreases, so the out-of-sample error U-shape is more pronounced than the in-sample one.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Moving from fixed to random design breaks the classical bias-variance tradeoff even in underparameterized, non-interpolating estimators.

record.problems: The linear-regression experiment uses one stated setting (n=100, σ=12, s=50); the k-NN experiment uses n=100 training examples and 100 test examples. Numerical curve values and uncertainty estimates are not provided in the text, and the plotted results do not report error bars.
record.rows_left_out: No results meeting the row criteria were omitted.

untested.parts: Sample size is not varied near the interpolation threshold.
Only linear regression is swept. Trees, boosting, kernels and random features are not run here.
No effective-complexity measure is used to predict where the peak falls.
Noise is varied only in the k-NN experiment, which has no interpolation peak. Regularization and multiple descent are not tested.
The effective-parameter U-turn result is cited from Curth et al. 2023 and not re-run here.

record.verdict_notes: A single simulation setting is used, with no error bars or numerical values in the text. The V7-relevant effective-parameter results are cited from the author's earlier work (Curth et al. 2023), not tested here. The limits_scope label rests partly on an analytic argument rather than only on measured values.

versions.untested_parts: No deep-network model-size sweep is conducted.
No sweep over training epochs or training time is conducted.
Training-sample size is not varied to measure test error near an interpolation threshold.
The paper tests a linear-regression feature-count sweep, not a broad range of model classes; it does not test deep networks, trees, or boosting as part of its own experiments.
The paper does not measure whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across axes.
It does not test whether label noise or regularization drives, splits, or removes double-descent peaks.
The effective-parameter-count account is discussed by reference to earlier work, but is not tested in this paper’s experiments.

rows.value: U-shaped for p≤n and constant for p>n; the text states interpolating models have in-sample prediction error 2σ².

rows.check: The state is correct. Note that the row combines the empirical curve (Fig. 4) with an analytic argument: any interpolating model has in-sample error 2σ² regardless of parameter count.
